Nutrition isn't in this year's lecture list — only its gift file exists, so this page is built from every gift (red), grouped by topic, with short added background boxes. There are no slides, notes or Aldughaither chapter.

1. Metabolic response to starvation and injury

Added explanationStarvation — early: glycogen runs out in ~24 h, glucagon rises to keep glucose up, and muscle protein is broken down for gluconeogenesis (urinary nitrogen high). Adaptation (days–weeks): the brain shifts to ketones, protein is conserved, metabolic rate falls and urinary nitrogen drops. Injury/stress — the opposite: catecholamines, cortisol and glucagon drive a hypermetabolic, catabolic state — raised metabolic rate, increased lipolysis, gluconeogenesis and protein breakdown (high urinary nitrogen loss), and peripheral insulin resistance → hyperglycaemia. The response is proportional to the tissue injury — laparoscopy blunts it.
  • Body's response to starvation → glucagon secretion increases to maintain blood glucose. 430
  • Response to injury compared with starvation → increased urinary nitrogen loss. 430
  • Neuroendocrine response to surgery → peripheral insulin resistance. 437
  • Necrotizing pancreatitis — physiological abnormality → increased lipolysis. 432 ×2
  • Right hemicolectomy — what helps the metabolic response → laparoscopic approach. 438 ×4 (Laparoscopy page)
Added explanationGhrelin — from the gastric fundus — is the hunger hormone (rises before meals; falls after sleeve gastrectomy). Leptin (fat) signals satiety. Absolute basal metabolic rate is higher in obese people (more total tissue to maintain). BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)².
  • Physiological action of ghrelin → hunger. 431
  • Basal metabolic rate of an obese vs normal-weight person → more than non-obese. 438
  • Formula for BMI → weight / height². 437 ×2 436

2. Nutritional assessment & who needs support

Added explanationAssessment: weight loss (> 10% in 6 months is significant), BMI, intake, and serum albumin (< 3.5 g/dL low; < 3.0 severe — predicts complications), with prealbumin/transferrin as shorter half-life markers. Support is indicated for a malnourished patient expected not to eat adequately for > 5–7 days, a well-nourished one for > 7–9 days, severe trauma or burns, and short bowel syndrome. If the gut works, use it — enteral first.
  • Gastric cancer before surgery — low blood level suggesting malnutrition → albumin. 430 ×2
  • Head-injured patient still in coma on day 5 — early feeding route → nasogastric tube (gut works; gastrostomy only for long-term feeding). 438 ×5
  • Cleft palate baby failing to gain weight before surgery → nasogastric tube feeding. 436
  • Mild acute pancreatitis → enteral feeding, IV fluids, pain control (no TPN, no antibiotics). 441
Added explanationParenteral nutrition only when the gut can't be used — massive small-bowel resection (short bowel), high-output proximal fistula, prolonged ileus/obstruction. Low-output fistulas (< 200 mL/day) with healthy distal bowel and no sepsis usually close on their own — keep feeding enterally.
  • Who will most likely need parenteral nutrition after surgery → massive small bowel resection for mesenteric ischaemia. 431 ×3
  • Obstructing lower oesophageal cancer with marked weight loss — pre-op nutrition → central parenteral nutrition (source key). 431 ×4
  • Enterocutaneous fistula < 100 mL/day, normal bowel, no fever → continue enteral feeding and wound care. 442
  • Crohn's patient after small bowel resection with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and malnutrition → short bowel syndrome (source key). 442

3. Complications of feeding

Added explanationRefeeding syndrome — feeding a starved patient (alcoholics, anorexia, prolonged fasting) triggers insulin release that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells → hypophosphataemia, weakness, confusion, arrhythmias, heart failure. Prevent by starting slowly with electrolyte (and thiamine) replacement.
  • Alcoholic not eating for 10 days, weakness, confusion and hypophosphataemia after feeding starts → refeeding syndrome. 442
Added explanationTPN complications: hyperglycaemia (concentrated dextrose) — a sudden rise despite insulin suggests sepsis; rebound hypoglycaemia if TPN is stopped abruptly; catheter sepsis (S. aureus → remove the line); thrombosis; electrolyte and liver problems.
  • Complication associated with TPN → hyperglycaemia. 438 ×8
  • On TPN with persistent hyperglycaemia despite insulin → check for a source of sepsis. 438 ×5
  • TPN stopped abruptly → anxiety, confusion, seizures → hypoglycaemia. 438 ×3
  • TPN via PICC, fever 39 °C, blood cultures grow S. aureus → remove the PICC, send the tip for culture and give antibiotics. 439 ×9

4. Special situations

Added explanationBurns raise metabolic needs more than any other injury — the Curreri formula: 25 kcal/kg + 40 kcal per %TBSA (adults). The recalled options don't match any formula exactly; the source keyed 70.
  • Caloric requirement in burn patients (recall) → 70 kcal/kg/% burn (source key; see the explanation). 438
Added explanationVitamins improve healing only when a patient is deficient — they do nothing for a well-nourished patient. After bariatric surgery, calcium and vitamin D absorption fall → vitamin D deficiency → secondary hyperparathyroidism.
  • Well-nourished patient given multivitamins after surgery → no effect on healing. 437 ×2
  • Symptoms of hyperparathyroidism 2 years after a gastric sleeve → vitamin D deficiency. 437
